analysis.one_liner: Bans mandatory arbitration and class action waivers in employer retirement and health benefit plans.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote, drawing no cosponsors before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the federal law governing employer retirement and health benefit plans (ERISA) to make mandatory arbitration clauses, class action waivers, and waivers of the right to have a lawyer or representative unenforceable. It would also stop plans from writing themselves discretion over benefit decisions, so courts would review disputed benefit denials from scratch. Workers could still choose arbitration after a dispute arises, but only voluntarily, in writing, after a 45-day waiting period. The bill was referred to committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees covered by employer retirement and health benefit plans would gain the right to take benefit disputes to court instead of being forced into arbitration, to join class actions alongside coworkers, and to have a judge review the plan's benefit decisions from scratch rather than defer to the plan's own interpretation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees in benefit plans

how_it_helps.text: It voids mandatory arbitration clauses written before any dispute arises, so workers and retirees could take benefit disputes to federal court under ERISA instead of a private arbitrator chosen under plan rules.
It voids class action waivers, letting groups of participants pool small individual claims — the kind of claim that is often too small to justify a lawsuit alone.

It voids 'discretionary clauses' that let plans give themselves final say over benefit decisions; courts would instead review disputed denials from scratch (de novo), removing the deference plans currently enjoy.

Post-dispute arbitration would still be allowed, but only if the worker agrees in writing after a 45-day waiting period, is told of the right to refuse, and faces no retaliation — a voluntary choice rather than a condition of the job or benefits.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, plan sponsors, and companies that administer retirement and health benefit plans would bear the cost: they could no longer force disputes into arbitration or block group lawsuits, so they would face more courtroom litigation over benefit claims, including class actions. Firms that profit from administering arbitration programs for benefit plans would also lose business.

drawbacks.text: Employers and plan sponsors argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for resolving benefit disputes, and that class actions over benefit plans drive up litigation and administrative costs that can be passed back to plans and participants through higher contributions or premiums.

Because individual ERISA benefit claims are often small, removing class action waivers may not reliably get workers to court in practice: without a class, many claims may still be too small for anyone to litigate, so the practical gain depends on group cases actually being brought.

The bill applies immediately to new disputes under existing plan documents, which would have created a one-year grace period only for updating paperwork, potentially producing a period of legal uncertainty over which clauses govern pending disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and retirees, the benefit is real: it removes three tools — forced arbitration, class action waivers, and self-granted plan discretion — that make it hard to challenge denied or mismanaged benefits. The honest cost is that employers would face more litigation, and some of that cost could be passed on to plans; and because many individual benefit claims are small, the gains depend heavily on workers actually being able to join group cases. On balance the bill is designed to shift leverage in benefit disputes from plan operators to participants.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 25, 2024, late in a two-year Congress, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it, leaving arbitration clauses and class action waivers in benefit plans unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, plan sponsors, and plan administrators that rely on mandatory arbitration and class action waivers to keep benefit disputes out of court are better off, because the restrictions never took effect.

for.name: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make arbitration clauses and class action waivers unenforceable in employee benefit plans, then saw it referred to committee with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No partisan split is visible: the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and never advanced far enough for any votes.

industries.industry: Employers and employee benefit plan sponsors
industries.note: The bill would bar them from forcing participants to arbitrate benefit disputes or waive class actions, exposing them to more courtroom litigation, including class suits over denied retirement and health benefits.

industries.industry: Plan administrators and third-party benefits processors
industries.note: These firms operate the arbitration and dispute-resolution machinery the bill would no longer let plans mandate, so restricting mandatory arbitration shrinks their role in benefit disputes.
Employment and benefits arbitration is a commercial market for arbitration providers; a ban on mandatory predispute clauses in benefit plans would remove a large category of forced cases.
